Core Clinical Tension: A distal lower extremity mass with initial plain radiographic features suggestive of a benign osseous exostosis, contrasting sharply with systemic constitutional symptoms (fever, weight loss, anorexia), markedly elevated inflammatory parameters (ESR, CRP), and CT findings of an aggressive-appearing pseudo-tumor with calcifications.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission clinical presentation concludes following the acquisition of initial imaging (plain radiograph and CT scan) and baseline inflammatory markers (ESR and CRP), immediately prior to bacteriological testing and histopathologic examination of the lesion.
3. Differential Distinctions: An osteochondroma/exostosis is ruled out by elevated inflammatory markers, lack of benign cortex-medulla continuity, and systemic symptoms; malignant bone sarcoma is excluded by the demonstration of caseating granulomas and positive bacteriological culture for Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
case_prompt:
A 32-year-old male presented with pain and swelling involving the distal third of the left thigh. He initially noticed a small swelling that had progressively increased in size, accompanied by a low-grade fever without diurnal variation, weight loss, and loss of appetite. He denied any preceding trauma to the site or other acute symptoms. He had no prior medical history of chronic illnesses or prior antimicrobial therapy, and there was no family history of chronic granulomatous infections.

On physical examination, an 80 × 40 mm, painful, firm mass was palpated in the left lower extremity that had gradually worsened. Motor and sensory examinations of the lower extremity were normal, and no lymphadenopathy was appreciated in the inguinal regions.

Plain radiography of the left thigh revealed a bony overgrowth with well-defined margins. A computed tomography (CT) scan demonstrated a 30 × 48 × 77 mm pseudo-tumor with irregular margins associated with calcifications. Laboratory evaluation showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 33 mm/hr and a C-reactive protein (CRP) of 80 mg/L.

diagnostic_reasoning.quote: CT scan showed a 30 mm x 48 mm x77 mm pseudo tumor with irregular margin associated with calcifications (C).

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The diagnostic breakthrough occurred when bacteriological examination demonstrated acid-fast bacilli positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis and histological analysis identified epithelioid giant cell granulomas with pathognomonic caseous necrosis, leading to complete clinical improvement on antitubercular therapy.
